authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Rose 1.5x; Land Area Alone Doesn't Explain The Harvest
authored_explainer.hook: Cereal production rose 1.5x; land area alone cannot explain the harvest.
says: Progression to secondary school rose from 77.8 in 1985 to 91.3 in 2017, 1.2 times higher. More students made the transition.
Cereal production rose from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 in 2024, 1.5 times higher. That means more grain.
Farmland: China 5.2, United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, Russia 2.2 million square kilometers. That is land area, not harvest size.
authored_explainer.closing: Food supply depends on what land produces, so acreage alone cannot explain what reaches the table.
authored_explainer.question: What best explains rising cereal production?

authored_explainer.title: Combustible Renewables And Waste Tripled In Share, Not Just Volume
authored_explainer.hook: Combustible renewables and waste reached 30.1% of the measured energy mix.
says: Combustible renewables and waste rose from 10.2% of total energy in 1990 to 30.1% in 2024, 3.0 times higher. Its share tripled.
Electricity access rose from 73.2% of the population in 1998 to 91.9% in 2024, 1.3 times higher. Access became much more widespread.
Waste methane (ch4) emissions rose from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 in 2024, 1.8 times higher. That still leaves emissions.
authored_explainer.closing: Energy from waste does not make waste harmless; its emissions still matter when comparing energy choices.
authored_explainer.question: How should waste energy account for emissions?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% While Cities Gained Share
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth fell 54%; slower growth still means a growing population.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% of the total in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025, down to 67 percent. Urban living gained share.
The largest city's share of urban population was 18.2% in 1972 and 16.2% in 2025, barely moved. Urban growth spread beyond it.
Population growth fell from 2 annual % in 1972 to 0.91 annual % in 2025, down to 46 percent. It continued more slowly.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower population growth changes planning needs, but it does not mean the population has started shrinking.
authored_explainer.question: How should cities prepare for slower growth?
